content_metadata.description: The video explores the importance of female role models in astronomy, focusing on how representation can inspire young girls and promote diversity within the field.

qAndA.answer: The girls are measuring a long white tube, likely a telescope tube, with a measuring tape.
qAndA.question: What activity are the girls doing at the beginning of the video?
Who does Theresa Summer say was Nichelle Nichols' biggest fan?

qAndA.answer: Nichols' role as Lt. Uhura in Star Trek served as a powerful role model for young black women, inspiring them to pursue careers in STEM fields like astronomy. This highlights the importance of representation and the impact it has on encouraging diversity and inclusion in science.
qAndA.question: How does the story of Nichelle Nichols connect to the overall theme of the video?

qAndA.answer: The video emphasizes that representation matters in astronomy. By sharing the stories of women who have made significant contributions to the field, we can inspire girls and create a more welcoming and inclusive environment for all.
qAndA.question: What is the main takeaway message of the video?

text_to_speech: Girls need to see themselves represented in Astronomy. and it actually turns out to be more important than you might think. Have you ever heard of the draw scientist experiment? Exploring back in 1966, the first decade of the test. Over 99% of the children drew male scientists. Over time there has been a great change in the children's drawings. We do a similar activity that's called 'Draw an Astronomer' Why do you think the children just aren't as likely to draw female Astronomers? We can't fix all of the problems that make science inaccessible for girls and women, but we can be part of the solution. Lemme tell you a story. How many of you watched the original Star Trek? If so, you probably know who this woman is. Nichelle Nichols She played Lieutenant Uhura She was one of the senior officers on the bridge. She went to a banquet, and she was told that she was going to meet her biggest fan. She thought it might be just another Trekkie but it turned out to be Martin Luther King Jr. He said it was the only show that he and Coretta would let his kids watch because she was an equal officer on the bridge of the enterprise. He told her that she was in a vital role not just as a model for the black children and young women across the country, but for all people who saw blacks and whites working together side by side. And he was right. Her role had important consequences. You may know this woman. Mae Jemison She was the first African-American female Astronaut. and she said, "As a little girl growing up in the south side of Chicago in the 60s I always knew I was going to be in space." She credits watching Lieutenant Uhura on the spaceship enterprise every week as her inspiration to reach for the stars. This story shows us the importance of role models and bringing more women into Astronomy. But if you can't role model? No problem! You don't have to be a woman to be a role model to girls. Even though I don't have first-hand knowledge of the experience of Black Americans, I can still tell that story about Nichelle Nichols and the importance of her role. And in the same way, it's important for you to sprinkle diverse stories of female Astronomers and Astronauts into your public engagement, to inspire the next generation of young women to feel welcome in Astronomy. Make sure that they see a space for themselves in Science. The truth is that there are many women who have contributed to the study of Astronomy, expanding our understanding of the Universe. Often these women have been overlooked or forgotten, but by telling their stories, we can show visitors that there's a place for everyone in Astronomy. When I show Saturn and someone asks me what the rings are made of, I tell them how Carolyn Porco discovered seven of the moons around Saturn as the head of the Cassini imaging team. and she had the nickname "The Queen of the Rings" because of her extensive knowledge of all those rings in the outer planets. And as the world expert on my favorite moon, Enceladus. I have long admired Annie Jump Cannon who was the estemeed Astronomer who came up with the system of classifying stars, like color and temperature. What's the story you often tell at the telescope or in response to a common question? See if you can work a woman's scientific contribution into one of your go-to stories. You'll never know who you inspire. Get your own inspiration from some of the sources listed below and make your public engagement more welcoming by telling the whole story.

youtube_description:
There are so many women who have contributed to our understanding of the Universe. Why not tell one of these stories the next time you are sharing the sky? 

Add these female astronomers to the stories you tell:
https://www.treehugger.com/female-astronomers-everyone-should-know-4864074
More resources are on the way!

Practice these techniques, share this video with your club, and find activities to do both on your own and as a club at the Night Sky Network:
https://nightsky.jpl.nasa.gov/download-view.cfm?Doc_ID=701

Find more techniques in our Confidence and Curiosity Video series:
https://youtube.com/playlist?list=PLjLQn63Cw1AJb1t9VxWRvAzDRRmHXEb8n
